title: AI will clone your game (if you're lucky) - a counterpoint to the fear and anxiety around making a game when AI exists.
author: Comet7777
selftext:
I keep seeing the same question here and in other dev communities: "Is it worth making a game today if AI can just copy it in a day?"  
  
People are pulling demos and skipping Next Fest over this. Those who haven't even built their game to get to those milestones are already paralyzed at the idea. 

Time for some tough love and some keepin' it real talk. No one is going to use AI to clone your game quickly, because no one knows your game even exists. Let me repeat that - you're scared of an outcome that has "successful launch/marketing" as a prerequisite.

Clones/copies don't follow ideas. They follow attention. Nobody spends their tokens cloning a game nobody has heard of. If you're worried about being cloned, you're worried about a problem that only shows up *after* you've solved the much harder problem of getting noticed.

But what about all of those viral posts about cloned games? So I went through the real cases I could find, and every one of them has the same thing in common: the game already had attention before it got cloned.

* Scale the Depths: won a game jam in 2024, blew up, then got flooded with clones. The devs said the clones partly fueled their success, because every clone pointed people back to the original.
* Zombies Aren't Real: cloned on Roblox before launch. But the dev already had two games out and a YouTube following, and his "I got cloned" video went viral and became his best marketing. (Garry Seto has a great breakdown.)
* Slotbound: cloned after the demo took off, worked with the storefronts to get the clones taken down, and still passed 200K copies in like 1-2 weeks (per the dev's own posts).
* Needle in a Haystack: search "needle" on Steam and you'll see the real downside. A breakout hit with an untrademarkable name is now surrounded by copycats. That's real, but it only happened because the original blew up first.
* Freya Holmer had a post blowup on Bluesky over a game idea. That post, alone, also blew up. Then the idea was copied. The bummer part about this story, however, is that the act of cloning her idea was enough to get her to stop working on it. 

So let's say somehow your game has the fundamentals down, it's fun, you're building a following, you've cut through the noise. Then what? Here's what you can actually do (some of these come from FlippedNormals' video on this, some come from me and my experiences):

1. Post the demo. No page, trailer or demo means nobody knows your game exists. "Scared money don't make money"
2. Ship demo-only builds. Don't put the full game in the demo behind a feature flag.
3. Build in public under your name. That paper trail of devlogs and feedback is your proof of who made it first.
4. Playtest with real people. Better game, more credibility, more recognition.
5. Layer your gameplay loops. A demo slice can't reveal what happens 10 hours in (think Pokémon: battles → gyms → the champion). If your whole game can be captured from a short demo... your game is lacking my dude. 
6. Keep detailed devlogs and talk about every milestone, including getting cloned.
7. Know trademarks and storefront report tools. Platforms can and do take clones down.

For now though, the focus and intention should solely be around making a good game, or treating this like a hobby. Any talk of getting your stuff stolen is totally premature. I made a longer video walking through all of this with the creators' breakdowns, if you want the deep dive: [https://youtu.be/iLBeUK\_mQW0](https://youtu.be/iLBeUK_mQW0)

comments.author: redskeletonbarbarian
comments.body: I'm not reading shit no one wrote

replies.author: DeanRayGames
replies.body:
And it's actually a really good post. I saw it over on vibecoding. You did good research, you presented it well, a "fair and balanced" take on how it helped some devs, and definitely hurt one or two, but overall, your point is cogent. Don't be afraid of AI cloning. If it happens to you, it'll probably be a good thing in the long run. 

And also implied: maybe don't name your game something that can't be copyrighted. Haha

comments.author: 4moves
comments.body: I've been making my game with the best AIs for 6 months now. Tweaking and Tweaking. I don't believe any AI will be able to make my game in a one shot. If they have the source. sure. Of course they could. How would you stop them. but There is a certain rule, that i constantly have to correct AI to force it to make my game. and i hope thats what will seperate good games from the slop. Its not what it looks like. Its what it does well. Im gonna start sharing some stuff soon. as i feel closer than ever.  I 've been testing with a small group of friends. and am about to start inviting trusted people to play it as well. Thanks for the video. Im looking for any tips i can get.

comments.author: Special_Animal2049
comments.body: AI is not sentient. AI doesn't act on its own and clone games randomly. Don't blame the tech for its user's intentions

comments.author: Woejack
comments.body:
I feel like this type of thing can only work for a friendslop type idea or something so small and simple in scope people can be fooled.

Look no further than the hundreds of vampire survivor clones, because that game is entirely exposed with a 10 minute glance.

I just don't see this type of thing working for anything with any narrative or artistic edge.

I see those components as an almost impenetrable defense against AI, and an excellent case for the power of human made art.

comments.author: HugoDzz
comments.body:
My [game](https://destroy.spritefusion.com/) hit 1M players after going viral and was cloned a lot since then. What worked for me:

\- No build in public.  
\- Drop it with network effects attached (in my case, a solid multiplayer mode).  
\- Prepare marketing upfront, and go fast once the game is released (updates, content etc).

The destroyed value is in attention damage because it's just a zero-sum thing.

replies.author: DeanRayGames
replies.body: Do any of the clones come close to being anything like your game, or even as fun?

replies.author: HugoDzz
replies.body:
It vary a lot actually, some are clearly low-effort clones, some are almost 1:1 clones. What made the difference was my multiplayer, which was kinda complex with anti-cheat, ranking system etc. so these part weren't in the client to strip out.

Overall, I feel it will be a bit like manufacture watches, there will be toys clones, and very "good" clones. The thing is the shape of the curve: it will be cheaper and cheaper to produce a good clone (time and money).
